title: Agentic AI workflows in anatomic pathology: Opportunities and challenges

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Agentic AI workflows in anatomic pathology: Opportunities and challenges》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction to LLMs · p0005】Large language models (LLMs) are now a familiar part of the information technology landscape, with products like ChatGPT (OpenAI) having among the fastest growing user bases in history.1 LLMs are a type of artificial intelligence (AI) system built using a machine learning architecture called a transformer. A key feature of the transformer is an attention mechanism that allows the model to assess the importance of words in a sequence relative to one another, permitting contextualization. When trained on vast amounts of data, LLMs demonstrate a remarkable ability to mimic understanding and generate human-like responses.2 LLMs excel at language processing tasks like document summarization, sentiment analysis, text classification, and text generation, which allows them to function remarkably well in the familiar role of a conversational chatbot.3

【Introduction to LLMs · p0010】In clinical medicine, LLMs have found utility in a broad range of applications such as clinical decision support,4, 5 clinical documentation,6, 7 chart summarization,8 ambient listening,9, 10 and provider–patient communication.11, 12 Additional applications adjacent to direct clinical care include matching patients to clinical trials,13 supporting medical coding workflows,14 automating hospital quality-measure abstraction and reporting,15 drafting prior-authorization letters,16 and extracting clinical research data from health records.17 Several of these features have moved beyond the research setting and are now deployed as commercial products in active clinical use. For example, Epic Systems Corporation (Epic) offers integrated LLM functions such as note summarization, LLM-extracted findings for radiology reports, AI charting, discharge summary drafting, encounter coding, patient-message responses, end-of-shift nursing notes, electronic prior authorization responses, and other clinician-facing text assistance.18

sections.text:

【Advanced LLM-related design patterns · p0050】The basic LLM design patterns described above can be extended by making software tools available to the models. Much of the practical utility of modern LLM systems comes not from the model alone, but from the software tooling built around it. A few of these design patterns are worth reviewing to build an understanding of how agentic AI can function.

【Future design patterns · p0895】As agentic systems mature, some workflows may involve multiple specialized agents rather than a single agent with every capability. For example, a pathologist-facing agent might coordinate with a departmental scheduling agent, a lab operations agent, or a vendor-hosted LIS agent. Google's Agent2Agent protocol has been proposed as an open standard for allowing agents built on different frameworks or vendor platforms to communicate, securely exchange information, and coordinate actions across enterprise systems.126 Multi-modal models create another path forward by allowing the same agentic system to integrate report text, clinical context, and whole-slide image data. Prior work has demonstrated pathology-specific question answering and report generation from whole-slide image inputs.41, 78 An agentic system could integrate such models as tools, creating very powerful and comprehensive end-to-end pathology workflows.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Agentic AI workflows in anatomic pathology: Opportunities and challenges》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusion · p0915】In radiology, where AI products are more mature and numerous than in pathology, peer-reviewed evaluations have found that some commercially available diagnostic AI products lack peer-reviewed evidence, that most supporting studies emphasize diagnostic accuracy rather than actual clinical outcomes, and, importantly, that real-world deployment requires (and can be delayed by) local validation, interoperability with PACS/RIS and EHR workflows, monitoring, governance, and management of clinical responsibilities beyond image classification.89, 136, 137, 138 Anatomic pathology shares many of the same challenges as radiology, so it is reasonable to expect a similarly prolonged and uneven adoption curve for pathology.

【Conclusion · p0910】The pace of clinical AI adoption has lagged behind some optimistic public speculation.132, 133 The prospect of transformative cost savings and efficiency gains from agentic AI has unsurprisingly generated a massive amount of interest.134 Recently, public comments from a prominent health care leader speculating about a reduced need for radiologists—if only regulatory barriers could be addressed—were reported in the mainstream press.135 Some of this bullishness is warranted; the diagnostic specialties do involve repetitive pattern recognition and computational tools can change the economics of how that work is performed. However, an overly reductionist view of what diagnostic physicians do should be viewed as a pitfall for administrators. Even at a remove from the bedside, creative problem-solving, open communication, emotional intelligence, nuanced judgment, compassion, and the irreducibly human act of caring are important. Economic forces will continue to push healthcare organizations toward automation, but the human costs of this transformation should be understood.

【Fig. 1 · f0005】Fig. 1 One-shot LLM interaction pattern. A user supplies a single prompt message, and the LLM generates a single text response.

【Fig. 2 · f0010】Fig. 2 Chatbot interaction pattern. A current user message and prior conversation context are assembled into the input sent to the LLM, which generates the next model response.

【Fig. 3 · f0015】Fig. 3 Retrieval-augmented generation pattern. A user request is used to retrieve relevant institutional context before prompt assembly and LLM response generation.
